2.text: of the same material (Fig. 61, d-g). Large pebbles are used for sinkers.
2.note: Small ink specks above the parenthesis after "d-g)" are bleed-through/offset from an adjacent line, not a diacritic on d or g — d-g is the italic figure-part label (Fig. 61, d through g), not a Tier-1 form. Confirmed at 4x.

3.text: They are strung on loops of thin leather, and, having no notch, easily fall

4.text: off. Pieces of bone or of walrus-ivory, with a strip of leather fastened through

5.text: a hole on the upper edge (Fig. 62, b), are also used for the purpose.
5.note: Machine draft (mz) misread the italic figure-part label "b)" as "6)" — confirmed at 4x it is a lowercase italic b, not a digit. Same bleed-through speck above the parenthesis as line 2, artifact not a mark.

6.text: Floats are made of wood, or of pieces of seal-intestines inflated with air

7.text: and carefully tied up (Fig. 62, a). The nets of the Russianized settlers on

8.text: the Kolyma and Anadyr, made of hemp or horsehair, are eagerly bought,

9.text: also Russian or American twine, cord, etc. On the small rivers the nets are

10.text: put across shallow places, and the fishes driven into them by men and boys

11.text: shouting, and by splashing the water a short distance farther along the stream.

12.text: Often two nets are joined together and used in seine fashion. Even parts of
12.note: Machine draft (mz) appended a trailing comma after "of" — confirmed at 2x the line ends bare, no comma. Not keyed.

13.text: tent-coverings are used to make the seine longer. Occasionally the whole seine
13.note: Machine draft (mz) appended a trailing comma after "seine" — confirmed at 2x the line ends bare, no comma. Not keyed.

14.text: will consist of a skin covering with a piece of net in the middle, in which to

15.text: catch the fish. These methods are used chiefly by the Reindeer people.

16.text: The Maritime Chukchee push their nets into the sea by means of a long

17.text: pole made up of two or three pieces joined together. A large stone is fas-

18.text: tened to the water end of the net with a strong piece of leather. The shore

19.text: end is tied to some stones or to a stake. These nets are used on the Pacific

20.text: for catching several species of Salmonidæ, such as humpback salmon (Oncorhyn-
20.note: Machine draft (mz) read the italic ligature as "Salmonide"; the raster shows æ (a-e ligature), keyed Salmonidæ.

21.text: chus horbusha), red salmon (O. lycaodon or niarka), and pink salmon (O. lagoce-
21.note: Machine draft (mz) misread lowercase italic l as capital I ("Iycaodon") and "horbusha" as "horousha"; both confirmed against the raster on the contact sheet.

22.text: phalus or keta); on the Arctic, for catching various species of Coregonus, such
22.note: Machine draft (mz) read "keta" as "heta"; confirmed "keta" on the contact sheet.

23.text: as Coregonus omul, C. leucichtys, C. maksun, C. nasutus, etc.

24.text: These nets are also set in the winter through holes cut in the ice with

25.text: ice-picks having stout iron points (formerly the points were made of bone).
